EMPLOYER IDENTIFICATION NUMBER (EIN) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Innovations LLC

EMPLOYER IDENTIFICATION NUMBER INFORMATION SHEET — PURPOSE AND SCOPE
This information sheet relates to Acme Innovations LLC, a Single-member LLC, regarding a federal Employer Identification Number (EIN) — the taxpayer identifying number the Internal Revenue Service assigns under 26 U.S.C. § 6109 and its implementing Treasury regulations. It describes what an EIN is, the federal rules that determine which entities and individuals are required or permitted to use one, situations in which an existing Social Security number or an already-issued EIN may continue to be used instead of a new one, how an EIN application is made, and a point of confusion the IRS's own published guidance directly addresses: when reorganizing or restructuring an existing entity does, and does not, require a new EIN. Jordan Lee is named below only as the individual this information sheet's declarations concern; naming that person here does not itself complete, sign, or submit IRS Form SS-4, Application for Employer Identification Number, or any other IRS filing, and this information sheet does not itself apply for, obtain, or record Jordan Lee's taxpayer identifying number (XXX-XX-XXXX) with the IRS. This document is not this project's LLC Articles of Organization, Articles of Incorporation, Statement of Information, Seller's Permit (CDTFA) Information Sheet, or Local Business License Information Sheet. Those documents concern separate filings and separate agencies; forming Acme Innovations LLC as a legal entity with the California Secretary of State, if Acme Innovations LLC is a corporation or LLC, is a distinct step that IRS guidance describes as ordinarily coming before an EIN application, not a step this information sheet performs. This information sheet also does not itself obtain an EIN for Acme Innovations LLC, does not determine whether Acme Innovations LLC's specific circumstances require an EIN, and does not constitute legal or tax advice.

THE EIN'S STATUTORY AND REGULATORY BASIS
Federal law requires that a person who must make a return, statement, or other document under the Internal Revenue Code include on it an identifying number the Secretary of the Treasury prescribes for that purpose. Treasury's implementing regulation identifies the Employer Identification Number (EIN) as one of several types of federal "taxpayer identifying numbers" — alongside the Social Security number, the IRS individual taxpayer identification number, and the IRS adoption taxpayer identification number — and gives it its own distinct numeric format, different from the Social Security-number format used for the other types. The same regulation states that these other identifying numbers are used to identify individual persons, while the EIN is used to identify employers and other nonindividual persons. This regulatory numbering scheme is the source of the EIN itself: an EIN is not a state-issued business registration number, a business license number, or a trade name registration; it is a number the IRS assigns under this specific federal statutory and regulatory authority.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Any person required under the authority of this title to make a return, statement, or other document shall include in such return, statement, or other document such identifying number as may be prescribed for securing proper identification of such person."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 6109(a)(1) (Cornell LII text), Statutory requirement to include a prescribed identifying number on a return, statement, or other document (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/6109)
  "Employer identification numbers take the form 00-0000000."
  — 26 C.F.R. § 301.6109-1(a)(1)(i) (Cornell LII e-CFR text), Treasury regulation defining the EIN's numeric form as one of several taxpayer identifying number types (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/26/301.6109-1)
  Known gap: This clause cites a statute and its implementing Treasury regulation, not two independent sources on the same question — the regulation exists to carry out the statute's own mandate, so the two citations corroborate one underlying authority rather than confirming it from separate directions. Both are hosted on law.cornell.edu's Legal Information Institute (LII), an unofficial but widely used repository of the U.S. Code and Code of Federal Regulations, drawn from (but not itself) the U.S. Government Publishing Office's official text; this clause was not separately checked against govinfo.gov's official text. This clause states only the identifying-number scheme's basic structure; it does not address every identifying-number type the same regulation covers, and it is informational only — it does not itself assign, apply for, or verify an EIN for any person.

WHICH ENTITIES AND INDIVIDUALS THE IRS SAYS NEED AN EIN
Treasury's identifying-number regulation draws a basic line by entity type: any person other than an individual — its own examples include corporations, partnerships, nonprofit associations, trusts, and estates — that is required to furnish a taxpayer identifying number must use an EIN, while an individual who is an employer or who conducts a trade or business as a sole proprietor is separately instructed to use an EIN as well. The IRS's own published guidance states the same basic rule in operational terms: an EIN is described as required for a business, organization, or certain retirement trust that has employees, that will need to pay employment, excise, or alcohol/tobacco/firearms taxes, or that withholds tax on certain income paid to a non-resident alien, and for an entity operating as a partnership, limited liability company, corporation, tax-exempt organization, estate, or trust (with an exception the same guidance states for certain grantor-owned revocable trusts), as well as a retirement plan or IRA, a real estate mortgage investment conduit, or a farmers' cooperative. That same IRS guidance adds that an entity that does not need an EIN for federal tax purposes may still request one for banking or state tax purposes.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Any person other than an individual (such as corporations, partnerships, nonprofit associations, trusts, estates, and similar nonindividual persons) that is required to furnish a taxpayer identifying number must use an employer identification number."
  — 26 C.F.R. § 301.6109-1(a)(1)(ii)(C) (Cornell LII e-CFR text), Treasury regulation requiring a nonindividual person required to furnish a taxpayer identifying number to use an EIN (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/26/301.6109-1)
  "You also need an EIN to operate any of these entities: Partnership Limited liability company (LLC) Corporation Tax-exempt organization Estate Trust"
  — IRS.gov, "Employer identification number" (Internal Revenue Service), IRS's own published list of entities that need an EIN to operate (https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/employer-id-numbers)
  Known gap: The regulation and the IRS's own guidance page are treated as two distinct sources here — the first is a legally binding Treasury regulation, the second is the IRS's own explanatory, non-binding guidance page — but both describe the same underlying rule, so this is corroboration of one settled point rather than two independently reached legal conclusions. The quoted IRS entity list is exactly the text of that page's bulleted list after removing its bullet formatting, not additional or paraphrased content. This clause does not repeat every item on the IRS's list in the citations below (retirement plans, IRAs, real estate mortgage investment conduits, and farmers' cooperatives are described in the body text above but not separately quoted), and it does not evaluate whether any specific person's or entity's activities actually trigger this requirement.

A SINGLE-MEMBER LLC OR SOLE PROPRIETOR MAY SOMETIMES USE AN EXISTING NUMBER INSTEAD OF A NEW EIN
Not every business needs its own separate EIN. Treasury's regulations state that, except as otherwise provided elsewhere in the same regulations, a business entity with a single owner that is "disregarded" as separate from that owner under the federal check-the-box entity-classification rules — the classification a single-member LLC receives by default unless it elects to be taxed as a corporation — must use its owner's own taxpayer identifying number for federal tax purposes, rather than obtaining a separate number for the LLC itself; for an individual owner, that identifying number is typically the owner's own Social Security number. The IRS's own published guidance on when a new EIN is required states a matching conclusion in practical terms for this situation: an existing sole proprietor's EIN may continue to be used for that person's single-member LLC, without obtaining a new EIN for the LLC, when the LLC has not elected to be taxed as a corporation or S corporation and does not have employees or an excise tax obligation. The same IRS guidance also marks the boundary of that rule: a single-member LLC does need its own, separate EIN once it must file excise or employment tax returns.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Except as otherwise provided in regulations or other guidance, a single owner entity that is disregarded as an entity separate from its owner under § 301.7701-3, must use its owner's taxpayer identifying number (TIN) for federal tax purposes."
  — 26 C.F.R. § 301.6109-1(h)(2)(i) (Cornell LII e-CFR text), Treasury regulation requiring a disregarded single-owner entity to use its owner's taxpayer identifying number (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/26/301.6109-1)
  "Use your sole proprietor EIN for your single-member LLC and don’t choose to be taxed as a corporation or an S corporation and don’t have employees or owe excise tax."
  — IRS.gov, "When to get a new EIN" (Internal Revenue Service), IRS's own guidance permitting a single-member LLC to continue using the sole proprietor's existing EIN in certain circumstances (https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/when-to-get-a-new-ein)
  Known gap: Both citations make the same underlying point from different sources — a binding Treasury regulation and the IRS's own non-binding guidance page — so they corroborate rather than independently establish it. This clause describes only the "disregarded entity" default classification that applies unless the LLC has affirmatively elected corporate tax treatment; it does not describe the check-the-box election mechanics themselves (26 C.F.R. § 301.7701-3), which are outside this clause's scope. This is informational only: it does not determine whether any specific single-member LLC has, or should have, its own EIN, and it does not address non-tax reasons — for example, a particular bank's own account-opening requirements — that may lead an LLC to obtain a separate EIN even when federal tax law alone would not require one.

COMMON POINT OF CONFUSION: ASSUMING EVERY BUSINESS REORGANIZATION REQUIRES A NEW EIN
A frequent point of confusion is whether reorganizing, converting, or otherwise changing the structure of an existing business automatically requires applying for a new EIN. Treasury's regulations state a general retention rule for one specific category of change: an entity that already has an EIN keeps that same EIN even when its federal tax classification changes under the check-the-box entity-classification regulations. The IRS's own published list of when a new EIN is, and is not, required goes further and gives specific examples for corporations on both sides of the line. That list identifies several situations as NOT requiring a new EIN — including changing a corporation's name or location, reorganizing to change only the corporation's identity or location, remaining the surviving corporation after a merger, converting at the state level without changing the underlying business structure, and electing to be taxed as an S corporation. By contrast, the same IRS list identifies other events — obtaining a new charter for the corporation from the secretary of state, becoming a subsidiary of another corporation, changing to a partnership or sole proprietorship, or merging in a way that creates a new corporation — as situations that do require a new EIN. Because the dividing line depends on which of these specific, IRS-enumerated events has occurred, an entity's own EIN is not something that resets automatically every time the entity's structure, ownership, or paperwork changes.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Any entity that has an employer identification number (EIN) will retain that EIN if its federal tax classification changes under § 301.7701-3."
  — 26 C.F.R. § 301.6109-1(h)(1) (Cornell LII e-CFR text), Treasury regulation providing that an entity retains its EIN when its federal tax classification changes (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/26/301.6109-1)
  "Reorganize to change only your identity or location."
  — IRS.gov, "When to get a new EIN" (Internal Revenue Service), IRS's own list identifying a corporate reorganization limited to identity or location as not requiring a new EIN (https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/when-to-get-a-new-ein)
  Known gap: The Treasury regulation cited below supports the narrower proposition that an EIN survives a change in federal tax classification specifically; the broader corporate examples in the IRS's own "When to get a new EIN" list — for example, remaining the surviving corporation after a merger, or converting at the state level — rest on that IRS guidance page itself rather than being separately traceable, word for word, to the cited regulatory text. The two citations are therefore best read as a binding regulation establishing the general retention principle for tax-classification changes, corroborated (not independently proven) by the IRS's own more detailed, non-binding illustration of that principle across a wider range of corporate events. This clause addresses only the corporation-specific portion of the IRS's list; the same IRS page states separate, differently worded rules for sole proprietorships, partnerships, LLCs, trusts, and estates that are not repeated here. This is informational only: it does not determine whether any specific entity's own reorganization or restructuring does or does not require a new EIN.

HOW AN EIN APPLICATION IS MADE, AND THE IRS'S OWN NO-FEE WARNING
An EIN is obtained by application, not automatically or by mere formation of a business. Treasury's regulations state that a person required to furnish an EIN must apply for one using Form SS-4, Application for Employer Identification Number, which is obtainable from any office of the Internal Revenue Service, a U.S. consular office abroad, or an IRS-authorized acceptance agent, and must be filed far enough in advance of the number's first required use to permit issuance in time for that use. The IRS's own current guidance describes its own online EIN tool as the way to get an EIN directly from the IRS, at no cost, within minutes of a successful application, available to a domestic organization whose principal place of business is in the United States or a U.S. territory and whose application is made by the entity's own responsible party or an authorized representative holding that party's Social Security number or individual taxpayer identification number; an applicant whose principal place of business is outside the United States must instead apply by phone, fax, or mail. That same IRS guidance states directly that applicants should be alert to non-IRS websites that charge a fee for an EIN, because obtaining an EIN from the IRS itself never carries a fee. Separately, the IRS's own guidance states that a person forming a corporation or LLC should register that entity with the state before applying for an EIN, and that EIN issuance through the IRS's online tool is limited to one EIN per responsible party per day; the cited guidance states this limit for the online tool specifically and does not say whether the same limit applies to an application made by phone, fax, or mail.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Any person required to furnish an employer identification number must apply for one, if not done so previously, on Form SS-4. A Form SS-4 may be obtained from any office of the Internal Revenue Service, U.S. consular office abroad, or from an acceptance agent described in paragraph (d)(3)(iv) of this section."
  — 26 C.F.R. § 301.6109-1(d)(2)(i) (Cornell LII e-CFR text), Treasury regulation requiring an EIN application on Form SS-4 (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/26/301.6109-1)
  "Use this tool to get an EIN directly from the IRS in minutes for free. Answer questions and submit the application. If it’s approved, we’ll issue your EIN immediately online. Beware of websites that charge for an EIN. You never have to pay a fee for an EIN."
  — IRS.gov, "Get an employer identification number" (Internal Revenue Service), IRS's own description of its free online EIN tool and its warning against fee-charging websites (https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/get-an-employer-identification-number)
  Known gap: The Treasury regulation and the IRS guidance page corroborate the same general point — that an EIN is obtained by application, historically on Form SS-4 — but the specific online-tool mechanics, its free-of-charge nature, the fee-scam warning, the form-your-entity-first sequencing, and the one-per-responsible-party-per-day limit described in this clause come only from the IRS's own guidance page, not from the cited regulatory text itself, which predates the online tool and speaks only in terms of the paper Form SS-4 process. This clause does not restate the regulation's separate provisions on international applicants, acceptance agents, or updating application information after an EIN is issued. The online tool's stated availability windows and other operational details reflect the IRS's guidance page as fetched on the date shown above and may change without updating this clause. This is informational only: it does not itself submit an EIN application for any person, and it does not determine whether a particular applicant qualifies to use the IRS's online tool.

CALIFORNIA'S EDD PAYROLL TAX ACCOUNT NUMBER IS A SEPARATE STATE NUMBER, NOT THE FEDERAL EIN
A federal EIN is not the same number as the account number the California Employment Development Department (EDD) issues to a registered California employer. California's EDD states that once an employer registers with EDD, the department issues its own eight-digit "employer payroll tax account number" — also called a State Employer Identification Number (SEIN) or State ID number — which is required for the employer's dealings with EDD, including filing state payroll tax returns and wage reports. EDD's own registration guidance separately instructs an employer registering for that state account number to include its federal EIN on the registration, explaining that doing so helps ensure the employer's state unemployment insurance tax payments are properly credited when the employer later files its federal unemployment tax return (IRS Form 940) with the IRS. An employer that registers with EDD therefore ordinarily holds two distinct numbers for two distinct purposes: a federal EIN issued by the IRS, and a separate state payroll tax account number issued by EDD; providing the EIN on an EDD registration does not substitute for, or duplicate, that separate state registration.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "After you register with EDD, you will receive an eight-digit employer payroll tax account number (example: 000-0000-0). This is also called a State Employer Identification Number (SEIN) or State ID number."
  — California EDD, "Step 3: Register for a Payroll Tax Account" (Employment Development Department), EDD's own description of the separate, EDD-issued state employer payroll tax account number (SEIN) (https://edd.ca.gov/en/payroll_taxes/step-3-register-for-a-payroll-tax-account/)
  "Include your Federal Employer Identification Number (FEIN) on your registration."
  — California EDD, "Step 3: Register for a Payroll Tax Account" (Employment Development Department), EDD's own instruction to include the federal EIN on state payroll tax account registration (https://edd.ca.gov/en/payroll_taxes/step-3-register-for-a-payroll-tax-account/)
  Known gap: Both citations below come from the same California EDD web page, not from two independent sources — this clause has only one primary source for the state-number side of this disambiguation. That page was fetched twice, using different request headers, to confirm its content was stable and not tailored to a particular requester, but that is a stability check, not independent corroboration from a second source. This clause does not address household-employer or other specialized EDD registration variants, does not state EDD's current registration fee, deadline, or online portal procedure (it is limited to the numbering distinction), and does not address any other state's analogous employer identification number, which may work differently. This is informational only: it does not register any employer with EDD and does not obtain a SEIN or EIN for any person.

CLOSING AND SIGNATURE BLOCK — EIN INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet regarding Acme Innovations LLC's federal Employer Identification Number was prepared by Jordan Lee.

Executed on September 2, 2026 at Sacramento, California.

Signature of Jordan Lee: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet describes the federal statutory and regulatory framework governing Employer Identification Numbers under 26 U.S.C. § 6109 and 26 C.F.R. § 301.6109-1, including which entities the IRS's own guidance identifies as needing an EIN, when an existing Social Security number or already-issued EIN may continue to be used instead of a new one, how an EIN application is made, the IRS's own warning that EIN issuance carries no fee, and California's separate EDD payroll tax account number. It is not IRS Form SS-4 or any other IRS or EDD form, does not itself apply for, obtain, or cancel an EIN or a California EDD account number for Acme Innovations LLC or any other person, does not constitute legal or tax advice, and does not determine whether Acme Innovations LLC's specific activities require an EIN. The current official EIN application tool and instructions are published by the Internal Revenue Service at IRS.gov.]

That same IRS guidance states directly that applicants should be alert to non-IRS websites that charge a fee for an EIN, because obtaining an EIN from the IRS itself never carries a fee. Separately, the IRS's own guidance states that a person forming a corporation or LLC should register that entity with the state before applying for an EIN, and that EIN issuance through the IRS's online tool is limited to one EIN per responsible party per day; the cited guidance states this limit for the online tool specifically and does not say whether the same limit applies to an application made by phone, fax, or mail.

citations.cite: Treasury regulation requiring an EIN application on Form SS-4
citations.quote: Any person required to furnish an employer identification number must apply for one, if not done so previously, on Form SS-4. A Form SS-4 may be obtained from any office of the Internal Revenue Service, U.S. consular office abroad, or from an acceptance agent described in paragraph (d)(3)(iv) of this section.

citations.case: IRS.gov, "Get an employer identification number" (Internal Revenue Service)
citations.cite: IRS's own description of its free online EIN tool and its warning against fee-charging websites
citations.quote: Use this tool to get an EIN directly from the IRS in minutes for free. Answer questions and submit the application. If it’s approved, we’ll issue your EIN immediately online. Beware of websites that charge for an EIN. You never have to pay a fee for an EIN.

expectedJSON.gap: The Treasury regulation and the IRS guidance page corroborate the same general point — that an EIN is obtained by application, historically on Form SS-4 — but the specific online-tool mechanics, its free-of-charge nature, the fee-scam warning, the form-your-entity-first sequencing, and the one-per-responsible-party-per-day limit described in this clause come only from the IRS's own guidance page, not from the cited regulatory text itself, which predates the online tool and speaks only in terms of the paper Form SS-4 process. This clause does not restate the regulation's separate provisions on international applicants, acceptance agents, or updating application information after an EIN is issued. The online tool's stated availability windows and other operational details reflect the IRS's guidance page as fetched on the date shown above and may change without updating this clause. This is informational only: it does not itself submit an EIN application for any person, and it does not determine whether a particular applicant qualifies to use the IRS's online tool.

expectedJSON.body: A federal EIN is not the same number as the account number the California Employment Development Department (EDD) issues to a registered California employer. California's EDD states that once an employer registers with EDD, the department issues its own eight-digit "employer payroll tax account number" — also called a State Employer Identification Number (SEIN) or State ID number — which is required for the employer's dealings with EDD, including filing state payroll tax returns and wage reports. EDD's own registration guidance separately instructs an employer registering for that state account number to include its federal EIN on the registration, explaining that doing so helps ensure the employer's state unemployment insurance tax payments are properly credited when the employer later files its federal unemployment tax return (IRS Form 940) with the IRS. An employer that registers with EDD therefore ordinarily holds two distinct numbers for two distinct purposes: a federal EIN issued by the IRS, and a separate state payroll tax account number issued by EDD; providing the EIN on an EDD registration does not substitute for, or duplicate, that separate state registration.

citations.case: California EDD, "Step 3: Register for a Payroll Tax Account" (Employment Development Department)
citations.cite: EDD's own description of the separate, EDD-issued state employer payroll tax account number (SEIN)
citations.quote: After you register with EDD, you will receive an eight-digit employer payroll tax account number (example: 000-0000-0). This is also called a State Employer Identification Number (SEIN) or State ID number.

citations.case: California EDD, "Step 3: Register for a Payroll Tax Account" (Employment Development Department)
citations.cite: EDD's own instruction to include the federal EIN on state payroll tax account registration
citations.quote: Include your Federal Employer Identification Number (FEIN) on your registration.

expectedJSON.gap: Both citations below come from the same California EDD web page, not from two independent sources — this clause has only one primary source for the state-number side of this disambiguation. That page was fetched twice, using different request headers, to confirm its content was stable and not tailored to a particular requester, but that is a stability check, not independent corroboration from a second source. This clause does not address household-employer or other specialized EDD registration variants, does not state EDD's current registration fee, deadline, or online portal procedure (it is limited to the numbering distinction), and does not address any other state's analogous employer identification number, which may work differently. This is informational only: it does not register any employer with EDD and does not obtain a SEIN or EIN for any person.
